candidates.attacker_control: The value of any `@Path`-annotated method parameter (after conversion through the configured string converter) is fully attacker-influenced whenever an application passes external input (user id, file name, key, redirect target, etc.) into such a parameter. This is a documented, mainstream usage pattern; the attacker does not need to control annotations or configuration, only one parameter value.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that (a) `{`/`}` are in PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET so an inserted value cannot introduce a new placeholder or recurse into another parameter's replacement, and `?`/`#` are always encoded so no query/fragment injection exists; (b) `String.replace` is literal (no regex injection); (c) `@Query(encoded=true)`/`@QueryMap` bypass of okhttp encoding is a separate, opt-in configuration issue and was not selected; (d) `RequestFactory` ordering rules (RequestFactory.java:352-377) do not validate values; (e) JAXB converter already disables XXE (JaxbResponseConverter.java:37-39), so the XXE lead was dropped; (f) header injection via @Header is mitigated by okhttp header validation; (g) OkHttpCall closes/consumes bodies for 2xx/204/205 and error paths, so no concrete leak was identified. Also considered that `encoded = true` is caller opt-in; however the snapshot contains no guard even for the non-opt-in `.`/`..` case, and the documented contract is one path segment, so the missing validation is a real defect rather than intended flexibility.
candidates.impact: An attacker-supplied path parameter can change the request target path on the same origin (e.g. requests meant for `/api/v1/...` reaching `/admin/...`, another tenant/version prefix, or paths that bypass path-prefix-based routing, gateway rules or server authorization assumptions). Because dot-segments are normalized before the request is sent, this is not merely cosmetic encoding. Secondary, lower-confidence consequence: when the placeholder is at the start of the relative URL and `encoded = true`, a value beginning with `//host/...` forms a scheme-relative reference and can change the resolved authority (host) of the request, i.e. redirect the call to an attacker-chosen host (SSRF-style). No weaponized reproduction is provided; impact is at the level of source-verified URL construction behavior.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) A service interface declares a method path containing a `{name}` placeholder with a corresponding `@Path` parameter and `encoded = true` (source-level evidence: this is the mode in which raw `/` and `%` pass through untouched, RequestBuilder.java:103,127); a bare `.`/`..` value can also escape one segment with the default `encoded = false` because `.` is never encoded. (2) The application routes untrusted data into that parameter. (3) The request is executed (OkHttpCall.createRawCall -> RequestFactory.create -> RequestBuilder.get), so the resolution/normalization step in okhttp runs. The attacker does not need any special privilege; this is client-side argument injection into the outbound request target.
candidates.root_cause: `RequestBuilder.addPathParam(String, String, boolean)` (RequestBuilder.java:89-95) replaces `{name}` in the relative URL with `canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded)` and performs no validation of the result. `canonicalizeForPath` (RequestBuilder.java:97-144) always percent-encodes only the set `PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET = " \"<>^`{}|\\?#"` (line 33); `.` (0x2E) is never in it, and `/` and `%` are explicitly skipped when `alreadyEncoded == true` (lines 103 and 127). Thus a path value such as `x/../y` (encoded=true) or a bare `..` (either mode) is inserted verbatim into `relativeUrl`, which is later resolved/normalized against the base URL via `baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl)` (line 149) or `baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl)` (line 197). The class contract is violated: `@Path` is documented as a "Named replacement in a URL path segment" (http/Path.java:28-31) and `@Path` javadoc explicitly tells users to set `encoded=true` for pre-encoded values (Path.java:40-49), but nothing verifies that the substituted value cannot alter path structure. The only path-related validation is annotation-time name validation (RequestFactory.java:372-374, 724-733); runtime argument values are never checked (RequestFactory.java:92-114).
candidates.title: `@Path` parameter values are substituted into the request URL without traversal validation, allowing path escape (path traversal) when `encoded=true` (and for `.`/`..` values with default encoding)
candidates.trace: 1) Interface method with e.g. `@GET("api/v1/files/{name}")` and `@Path(value = "name", encoded = true)`. 2) At parse time RequestFactory.Builder.parseParameterAnnotation (RequestFactory.java:352-377) builds `ParameterHandler.Path(name, converter, path.encoded())`; only the placeholder name is validated (lines 724-733). 3) At call time RequestFactory.create applies each handler (RequestFactory.java:102-109) -> ParameterHandler.Path.apply (ParameterHandler.java:94-100) -> RequestBuilder.addPathParam (RequestBuilder.java:89-95). 4) addPathParam calls canonicalizeForPath(value, true): `/` and `%` are excluded from encoding by the `!alreadyEncoded` guard (lines 103/127), and `.` is not in PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET, so `../` sequences survive verbatim; the value is inserted with String.replace (line 94) and no post-check. 5) RequestBuilder.get() (lines 189-202) either builds `baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl)` earlier (line 149, when any `@Query` parameter exists) or calls `baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl)` (line 197). OkHttp resolves the relative reference per normal link semantics (documented in Retrofit.java:461-519), including RFC-3986 dot-segment removal, so `api/v1/files/../../admin` resolves outside the intended `/api/v1/files/` prefix. 6) The traversed URL is attached to the OkHttp request (RequestBuilder.java:226-228) and sent. Search of the whole snapshot for `traversal`/`PATH_TRAVERSAL`/`shouldn't` found no counter-check anywhere; the two test files that would cover this behavior are absent (RequestBuilderTest.java missing; RequestFactoryAndroidTest.java:28 still imports the removed RequestFactoryTest).
candidates.unverified: The final dot-segment normalization happens inside the external okhttp 3.11.0 dependency (declared in pom.xml:53), which is not part of this snapshot and could not be inspected; the conclusion that `HttpUrl.resolve`/`newBuilder(String)` remove `.`/`..` segments relies on the repository's own documentation (Retrofit.java:461-519: endpoint values are resolved with `HttpUrl#resolve(String)` and "matches that of an <a href=""> link on a website resolving on the current URL") plus standard RFC-3986 resolution. The exact behavior for percent-encoded dot segments (`%2e%2e`) and for the `//host` authority-swap variant was not verified. No code was executed and no request was sent, so exploitability in any particular application (which depends on that application's use of `@Path(encoded=true)` with untrusted data) is not confirmed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 (path traversal) / improper neutralization of path segments in the outbound request URL (request-target injection)

coverage_summary: Visible scope: 293 files (294 at root, 1 excluded by sensitive-name/path filter, 0 symlinks/binary refusals); the P1 index parsed 234 Java files (2,960 symbols, 10,084 call sites, 8498 unresolved calls) and reports 11 omitted files and no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution. I read the core `retrofit` module in depth (RequestFactory, RequestBuilder, ParameterHandler, Retrofit, ServiceMethod/HttpServiceMethod, OkHttpCall, Utils, Platform, Call/Response/Converter and all http/ annotations), plus the JAXB/SimpleXML/Gson converter sources and the mock module's error paths; I sampled the adapter modules (guava/java8/rxjava/rxjava2/scala) and did not exhaustively review every converter variant, sample, or the website assets. The two core test files that exercise request-URL construction (RequestBuilderTest.java, RequestFactoryTest.java) are not present in the snapshot (RequestFactoryAndroidTest.java:28 references the missing RequestFactoryTest.buildRequest), so their assertions could not be used as counterevidence. All statements about the finding are based on the visible source; no runtime or dependency-level verification was possible.
limitations: okhttp 3.11.0 is an external dependency not present in the snapshot; the actual dot-segment/authority resolution of `HttpUrl.resolve` and `HttpUrl.newBuilder(String)` was not verifiable in-source (inferred from Retrofit.java:461-519 javadoc and RFC-3986 semantics).

P1 index provides syntax candidates only: no data-flow, control-flow, semantic resolution or reachability proof (8,498 unresolved calls; 11 omitted files). The candidate trace was assembled by manual reading of the cited source lines.

Test files covering request building (RequestBuilderTest.java, RequestFactoryTest.java) are missing from the snapshot, so no in-repo negative/positive test could confirm or falsify the traversal behavior.
No code, tests or scanners were executed and no network requests were made; all findings are source-level leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.
Conversion by user-supplied string converters could produce the same dangerous values for an `@Path` parameter; the review assumes the common case where the raw String value reaches the builder.

rejected_leads.lead: Arbitrary absolute URL via `@Url` parameter (possible SSRF) in ParameterHandler.RelativeUrl -> RequestBuilder.setRelativeUrl (ParameterHandler.java:57-62, RequestBuilder.java:73-75).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of `@Url` (RequestFactory.java:319-350 requires an explicit @Url parameter); the library intentionally resolves it against the base URL including absolute/relative links. No missing-validation defect inside the library can be pointed to, so it is not a vulnerability of this codebase.

rejected_leads.lead: Query/field parameter injection through `encoded = true` (`&`/`=` pass through in okhttp `addEncodedQueryParameter`, RequestBuilder.java:157-163).
rejected_leads.reason: Explicit, documented opt-in ('parameter name and value are already URL encoded', http/Query.java:77-80); lower security impact than the selected candidate and arguably intended behavior. Kept only as a related observation.

JaxbResponseConverter explicitly sets IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false and SUPPORT_DTD=false (JaxbResponseConverter.java:37-39). SimpleXmlConverterFactory delegates to the third-party org.simpleframework.xml Persister; no source-level retrofit defect or version evidence of a vulnerable parser configuration was found in the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Platform.Java8.invokeDefaultMethod uses a trusted MethodHandles.Lookup (-1) to invoke non-public interface default methods (Platform.java:96-106).
rejected_leads.reason: Local-JVM reflective behavior; no attacker-controlled input crosses a trust boundary here, and it is standard well-known technique for default-method dispatch. No security impact demonstrated.
Error bodies are buffered and closed, 204/205 close the body, and converted bodies are closed by converters; no concrete leak or injection was identified in source.

summary: Retrofit 2.4.1-SNAPSHOT (square/retrofit, 293 visible files). Review focused on the core request-construction trust boundary (annotation parsing -> parameter handlers -> URL building). I found no validation anywhere in the snapshot that a `@Path` value stays inside its annotated path segment: `RequestBuilder.addPathParam` does a plain `String.replace` of the placeholder with a value that is only percent-encoded for a fixed character set, and `.`/`/`/`%` are deliberately left untouched when `encoded = true` (and `.` is never encoded at all). The resulting relative URL is then resolved/normalized against the base URL (`baseUrl.resolve(relativeUrl)` / `baseUrl.newBuilder(relativeUrl)`), so `..`-segments and raw slashes supplied for a path parameter can remove/replace path segments of the final request URL. This is a path-traversal / request-target injection defect in the library's URL-building path (CWE-22 family), reachable whenever an application forwards untrusted data into an `@Path(encoded = true)` parameter (or passes `.`/`..` with default encoding). I could not find the corresponding negative tests in the snapshot (`retrofit/src/test/java/retrofit2/RequestBuilderTest.java` is absent, and `RequestFactoryAndroidTest.java:28` has a dangling `import static retrofit2.RequestFactoryTest.buildRequest;`), so the behavior could not be re-checked against existing assertions. No runtime confirmation was performed.
